title: Chicken breast, fried, coated, skin/coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast that has been deep‑fried in a crispy coating, served without the edible skin or coating. It is a common item on fast‑food and quick‑service restaurant menus, often presented as strips or nuggets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Deep‑frying at 175‑190 °C creates a golden, crunchy crust.
The coating is usually a mixture of flour, breadcrumbs and spices, but it is often discarded by diners who prefer the meat only.
Raw chicken breast is one of the leanest cuts of poultry, yet frying adds a substantial amount of calories.
In the United States this product is frequently called "Chicken Tenders" or "Chicken Strips".
In some countries the coating is served on the side, allowing customers to choose whether to eat it.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides about 31 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Low fat in the raw meat
items.content: Raw breast contains less than 3 g of fat per 100 g, though much of it is absorbed during frying.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B3 (niacin) and B6 aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports immune health and thyroid function.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The high protein content helps keep you feeling full for longer.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds significant calories and fat, which can contribute to weight gain if consumed frequently.

items.title: Trans and saturated fats
items.content: Using old or repeatedly heated oil can introduce trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: The coating often contains salt and flavor enhancers, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Wheat allergy / gluten
items.content: The breading typically includes wheat flour, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen; moderate consumption is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried chicken breast strips are usually served hot with dipping sauces such as barbecue, ranch, or honey‑mustard. They can be eaten as a snack, added to salads, sandwiches, or wraps, and the coating can be removed if a lower‑calorie option is desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked product refrigerated at 0‑4 °C and consume within 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.
